Aionios
ai-OH-nee-os
adj. (Greek)
Greek aiōnios, “eternal, age-long, of-the-age,” from aiōn (age, eon). The adjective carries both qualitative (pertaining to the eschatological age) and quantitative (everlasting, unending) senses, depending on context.

📖 Biblical Definition

Aiōnios is the New Testament’s great adjective for eternal, and it carries some of the heaviest doctrinal freight in the Bible. The word is built from aiōn (age, eon), and its semantic range covers both the qualitative sense (pertaining to the coming age, the age-to-come, the eschatological age) and the quantitative sense (everlasting, unending in duration). Both senses are biblically operative, and the contexts make clear which is foreground in each use. Aiōnios qualifies several of the New Testament’s most weighted nouns. Eternal life (zōē aiōnios): the great gospel-promise word, used over forty times in the NT, especially in John’s Gospel and Epistles; John 3:16 (that whosoever believeth in him should not perish, but have everlasting life); John 10:28 (and I give unto them eternal life); 1 John 5:11 (God hath given to us eternal life, and this life is in his Son). Eternal punishment (kolasis aiōnios): Matt 25:46 (and these shall go away into everlasting punishment: but the righteous into life eternal)—the same adjective applied to both punishment and life in the same verse, making it grammatically untenable to read aiōnios as everlasting for the life and temporary for the punishment. Eternal fire (pur aiōnios): Matt 18:8; 25:41; Jude 7. Eternal destruction (olethros aiōnios): 2 Thess 1:9. Eternal God: Rom 16:26 (the eternal God); Heb 9:14 (the eternal Spirit). Eternal gospel: Rev 14:6. Eternal weight of glory: 2 Cor 4:17. Eternal covenant: Heb 13:20. Eternal kingdom: 2 Pet 1:11. Eternal inheritance: Heb 9:15. The grammar of aiōnios is therefore structurally important for several theological doctrines. The eternality of God (the eternal God; the eternal Spirit) is non-negotiable. The eternality of the gospel-given salvation is the believer’s great hope. The eternality of the punishment of the impenitent is the sober counterpart, against universalist readings that would make aiōnios kolasis a temporary corrective rather than an everlasting condition (the same word applied to life cannot mean different durations in the same Matthew 25:46). The category of the age to come, marked by aiōnios, is the structural eschatological category: the present age (this aiōn) is passing; the age to come is everlasting; the saints belong to the age to come and live in this age as those whose home and inheritance are in the next.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

(Greek term.) Aiōnios: eternal, everlasting, of-the-age-to-come; the great NT adjective qualifying life, punishment, God, gospel, weight of glory, covenant, kingdom, and inheritance; carries both qualitative (eschatological) and quantitative (everlasting) senses.

ETERNAL, a. — 1. Without beginning or end of existence. 2. Without beginning of existence. 3. Without end of existence or duration; everlasting; endless. 4. Perpetual; ceaseless; continual. In scripture, applied to God (the eternal God), to the punishment of the impenitent (everlasting punishment), to the life of the redeemed (eternal life), and to many other nouns.

AIONIOS — (Greek adjective, G166.) Eternal, everlasting, age-long; 71 NT uses. Qualifies life (zōē aiōnios) over 40 times; also punishment (Matt 25:46), fire (Matt 18:8), destruction (2 Thess 1:9), God (Rom 16:26), Spirit (Heb 9:14), gospel (Rev 14:6), weight of glory (2 Cor 4:17), covenant (Heb 13:20), kingdom (2 Pet 1:11), inheritance (Heb 9:15).

📖 Key Scripture

John 3:16 — "For God so loved the world, that he gave his only begotten Son, that whosoever believeth in him should not perish, but have everlasting life."

Matthew 25:46 — "And these shall go away into everlasting punishment: but the righteous into life eternal."

2 Corinthians 4:17 — "For our light affliction, which is but for a moment, worketh for us a far more exceeding and eternal weight of glory."

Romans 16:26 — "But now is made manifest, and by the scriptures of the prophets, according to the commandment of the everlasting God, made known to all nations for the obedience of faith."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

Aiōnios is corrupted, on one side, by the universalist readings that would make aiōnios kolasis (eternal punishment) mean age-long corrective against the grammatical parallel with aiōnios zōē (eternal life) in the same Matt 25:46—and on the other by the present-age-only register that has lost the eschatological weight of the age to come as the structural orientation of Christian life.

expand to see more

The universalist corruption of aiōnios attempts to read eternal punishment in Matt 25:46 as merely age-long corrective—a temporary purifying discipline from which the recipient eventually emerges purified. The grammatical move is untenable: the same adjective in the same verse qualifies both punishment and life; if aiōnios in life eternal means everlasting (as universalists typically concede, since they want the saints to have everlasting life), then aiōnios in everlasting punishment must mean everlasting too—and the universalist reading collapses on its own grammar. The same adjective cannot mean two different durations in the same verse depending on which noun the interpreter prefers. The orthodox tradition has therefore consistently read aiōnios kolasis as everlasting punishment—a sober doctrine, not lightly preached, but biblically grounded and structurally bound to the eternality of the corresponding life it stands against. The recovery of the doctrine is the recovery of the gospel’s seriousness: the offer is real, the warning is real, and both run the same eternal duration the same Greek adjective names.

The opposite corruption is the present-age-only register that has lost the eschatological weight of the age to come as the structural orientation of Christian life. The category aiōnios in many of its NT uses carries the qualitative sense (pertaining to the age-to-come, the eschatological age) alongside the quantitative sense (everlasting); both belong to its meaning. Contemporary preaching often loses both. The believer is not regularly oriented toward the age to come as the home and inheritance to which the present age is the antechamber; the eschatological future is bracketed; the Christian life becomes a present-age project of personal flourishing rather than a pilgrimage toward the consummating age. Recover the doctrine, and the saint recovers his proper orientation: this present age is passing, the age to come is everlasting, the saint belongs to the age to come and lives in this age as a sojourner whose home is elsewhere. The eternal weight of glory of 2 Cor 4:17, the eternal inheritance of Heb 9:15, the eternal kingdom of 2 Pet 1:11—these are not vague hopes for after-death continuity but the substantive realities of the age to come that aiōnios names with both qualitative and quantitative weight.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek aiōnios (eternal, everlasting, of-the-age-to-come), from aiōn (age, eon); qualifies the NT’s great nouns (life, punishment, fire, destruction, God, Spirit, gospel, weight of glory, covenant, kingdom, inheritance) with both qualitative (eschatological) and quantitative (everlasting) weight.

expand to see more

Greek aiōnios (G166) — eternal, everlasting (71 NT uses).

Greek aiōn (G165) — age, eon (the etymological root; both the present age and the age to come).

Hebrew ‘ōlām (H5769) — everlasting, eternity (the OT equivalent; the LXX translates with aiōn/aiōnios).

Greek aidios (G126) — everlasting (the cousin adjective; used of God’s eternal power and Godhead, Rom 1:20).

Usage

"And these shall go away into everlasting punishment: but the righteous into life eternal—the same adjective qualifies both nouns; the grammatical parallel grounds the duration of both equally."

"The age to come, marked by aiōnios, is the structural eschatological category: the present age passes, the age to come is everlasting, the saints belong to the age to come."

"Universalist reading collapses on the Matt 25:46 grammatical parallel; present-age-only reading loses the eschatological orientation; biblical aiōnios carries both qualitative and quantitative weight in every use."
